# Digital filtering: moving average and IIR: the exercise

<!-- Generated by tools/maintainer/build_exercise_readmes.py from the lesson page. Edit the lesson, then run the script. -->

Lesson: [Digital filtering: moving average and IIR](https://jouhis.github.io/embedded-course/lessons/0107-digital-filtering.html). Read it first: the steps below refer to its diagrams and worked examples.

## Try it: the Pico filter on a noisy reading

The Wokwi potentiometer is perfectly steady, so the simulator shows no noise. The project `projects/0107-filter-pico` adds a seeded pseudo-random noise of about ±16 codes and a spike of 600 codes on every 25th sample, then prints one CSV row per sample: time, raw, median, moving average and EMA. The first printed line is `FILTER OK`, the second is the header `ms,raw,median,ma8,ema`, and a row follows every 50 ms.

1. Copy your finished `ma_update`, `ema_update` and `median3_update` from the host project into `projects/0107-filter-pico/starter/filters.c`, keeping the init functions that are already there.
2. In `starter/main.c`, replace the three placeholder lines `m = raw`, `a = raw` and `e = raw`. Run `median3_update` on `raw` first. Then pass the median output to both `ma_update` and `ema_update`, so the two smoothers run side by side on the same de-spiked signal, which is what the CSV columns compare. The reference solution does exactly this, and the starter's comment describes it as a chain.
3. Print `FILTER OK` once, before the loop starts, as the reference solution does. The starter's comment asks for it after the eight-sample window fills. Either version prints the text that the automatic check looks for.
4. Build with <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>B</kbd>, then <kbd>F1</kbd> → *Wokwi: Start Simulator*. The serial monitor should show `FILTER OK`, then the header, then rows every 50 ms. The spike rows are at 1250 ms and 2500 ms: their `raw` column is about 600 codes higher than its neighbours, and their `median`, `ma8` and `ema` columns barely move. The 0 ms row is the exception. The median has no full window at start-up, so it passes its first inputs through, and the spike shows in the `median` column on that first row.
5. Copy the CSV from the serial monitor into a file and plot the columns, or paste it into a spreadsheet. To see what the spike does to an average, change one line in `main.c` so that `ma_update` takes `raw` instead of `m`, rebuild, and look at `ma8`. It now rises by about 75 codes for eight rows after each spike, because 600 ÷ 8 = 75. Change the line back before you go on.
